Arc: the draft said the IMF links the 2009–2016 growth to record fishing licence fees. 'Stalled in 2020' became 'barely grew in 2020 as COVID travel limits hit', which the IMF 2021 press release supports.

growth_story.headline: Income per person in the Marshall Islands, flat from 1990 to 2008, grew 5.2 percent a year in 2017–2025, led by fishing and construction.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in the Marshall Islands barely moved from 1990 to 2008, growing 0.1 percent a year, and it ended that era about where it began. The IMF ties the mid-1990s slump, with falls of 11.2 percent in 1996 and 7.4 percent in 1997, to shrinking grants and the need to repay debt the government had borrowed against future Compact money. Growth rose to 2.9 percent a year in 2009–2016, when, the IMF says, delayed infrastructure projects got going and fishing licence fees reached record highs. From 2017 to 2025 it reached 5.2 percent a year, against 1.4 percent in the decade to 2015, led by fishing and construction: income per person jumped 13.7 percent in 2019, barely grew in 2020 as COVID travel limits hit, and dipped 2.3 percent in 2023. It rose 6.8 percent in 2024 and 5.9 percent in 2025, reaching its highest level so far.

threads.title: Grant cuts and the 1990s slump
threads.text: After nearly a decade of growth following independence in 1986, the economy shrank in the mid-1990s as grants fell and the government repaid debt it had borrowed against future Compact money. Income per person dropped 11.2 percent in 1996 and 7.4 percent in 1997, and by 2008 it was no higher than in 1990.

threads.title: A larger new Compact
threads.text: A new 20-year Compact with the United States began in FY2024 with more money than the last one. In August 2025 a universal basic income and a second cash scheme, the Extraordinary Needs Distribution, were approved, both paid for from the Compact Trust Fund, and the IMF expects them to lift growth in FY2026.

threads.title: People keep leaving
threads.text: Under the Compact, Marshallese can work and study in the United States without a separate permit, and the pull of higher wages there has long thinned the pool of skilled workers at home. The IMF expects continued emigration of workers to hold back growth in the years ahead.

since_last_year.text: The new cash schemes were approved in August 2025, and in December 2025 the IMF expected growth to speed up in FY2026. Then disruption in world energy markets in 2026 tripled fuel costs and sharply raised the fuel import bill. In June 2026 the World Bank said fishing, the largest source of export earnings and government revenue, was expected to decline and that growth in FY2026 would now slow. The ADB's September 2026 outlook expects only modest growth in 2026 and 2027.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes total output shrinking in FY2020 under COVID travel limits, falling in FY2022 and FY2023, and growing modestly in FY2024. The data instead show income per person edging up in 2020, rising 2.5 percent in 2022, falling only 2.3 percent in 2023 and rising 6.8 percent in 2024. The IMF's estimate of total output growth in FY2019 is also well below the 13.7 percent rise in income per person that year. Fiscal and calendar years differ, and the figures may come from different data releases. The ongoing emigration the IMF describes would also let income per person rise faster than total output, so part of the climb since 2017 may reflect fewer people rather than much more output.
